sections.h2: Who runs property tax in Peoria County, Illinois?
sections.html:
Four offices share the work in Peoria County. The Treasurer doubles as County Collector and sends the bills, the Supervisor of Assessments oversees valuation, the Board of Review hears complaints, and the County Clerk calculates rates and takes redemption payments on sold taxes. A township assessor stands first in line for any question about what your house is worth.

Peoria County sits on the Illinois River in central Illinois. It was formed in 1825 out of Fulton County and covers 631 square miles, with the city of Peoria as county seat. Peoria and West Peoria are treated as independent of the surrounding townships, so a house in either place deals with a city township office while a rural parcel deals with its own township.

  • Treasurer: bills and collects real estate tax at 324 Main Street, Room G15, in the courthouse.
  • Supervisor of Assessments: publishes assessment changes and handles exemption questions at 309-672-6910.
  • Board of Review: a three-member panel appointed by the County Board, at Room 301 of the courthouse.
  • County Clerk: extends the tax rate and receives payment of sold taxes at Room 101.

sections.h2: What does the Peoria County housing market look like for a seller with tax questions?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table estimates 178,553 residents for July 2025, about 1.9% fewer than the April 2020 base. The county has 84,884 housing units and 77,755 households. Owners occupy 67.0% of homes, and the median value of an owner-occupied unit for 2020-2024 is $158,500.

Median gross rent runs $993 a month and median household income is $65,108. Health care and social assistance is the largest line among the economic figures QuickFacts lists, with receipts of about $3.9 billion for 2022, which fits the hospital cluster in the city of Peoria.

Winters are cold: Wikipedia puts the average January low at 14 degrees Fahrenheit and the July high at 86.

sections.h2: When is Peoria County property tax due and what happens if you pay late?
sections.html:
Peoria County issues one bill a year and splits it into two equal installments. For 2025 taxes, payable in 2026, the due dates were June 9 and September 9, 2026, and the county planned to mail bills by May 1. The Treasurer says a missing bill does not excuse the payment, and asks owners who have no bill by May 15 to call 672-6065, option 5.

The county page states there is no grace period. A payment postmarked or received after the due date carries a penalty of 1.5% per month or part of a month. A postage meter imprint is not accepted as proof of timeliness, and the Treasurer notes the Peoria postal facility no longer applies postmarks.

  • Cash, personal checks, cashier's checks and money orders work in person or by mail, but never send cash in an envelope.
  • Online and phone payments open after May 1. Cards, Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal and Venmo carry a 2.65% convenience fee, and an electronic check costs $1.00.
  • Phone payments add $0.95 per parcel, and none of the processing fees go to the county.
  • A check returned by the bank costs $25.00.
  • Partial installments are sent back, so each payment has to cover the full installment plus any penalty.

sections.h2: What dates matter on the 2025 Peoria County tax calendar?
sections.html:
The table below lists the dates the county published for the 2025 tax year. All of them have now passed, but the same sequence repeats every year with shifted dates.

Peoria County calendar for 2025 taxes payable in 2026, from county Treasurer and Board of Review pages
StepDate posted by the county
Tax bills mailedBy May 1, 2026
First installmentJune 9, 2026
Second installmentSeptember 9, 2026
Board of Review filing deadlineSeptember 30, 2026
Final notices of unpaid tax mailedNo later than October 12, 2026

After final notices go out, the collector adds $10 for registered mail and newspaper publication, and the county page lists a further $113 at the time of sale. Ask the Treasurer for the exact payoff before you wire money.

sections.h2: How do assessments and appeals work in Peoria County?
sections.html:
Property is valued as of January 1, and the 2026 notice to taxpayers gives a required assessment level of 33.33% of fair market value against a county median level of 31.25%. The Supervisor of Assessments applies an equalization factor to each township's classes of property, then the bill uses the equalized value less exemptions multiplied by the tax rate.

The county urges you to speak with your township assessor before filing anything. If you still disagree, a Board of Review complaint can be filed from June 1 until 30 days after your township's changes appear in the newspaper. For 2026 the Board of Review page lists a filing deadline of September 30, so that window has closed and the next one opens June 1 of the following year.

  • A complaint is not a tax protest. It questions the assessment and affects the next bill, not the one you already hold.
  • Evidence should go in with the complaint form, and the Board may raise, lower or leave the value alone.
  • If you miss your hearing, the case is decided on what you filed, and hearings cannot be rescheduled.
  • Complaint packets are on the county's Forms and Documents page, and mailed filings go to Room 301 of the courthouse.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can lower a Peoria County tax bill?
sections.html:
Most of the relief programs lower the equalized assessed value rather than the bill itself, so the savings depend on the tax rate for your district. The Supervisor of Assessments lists these on its Tax Relief page.

  • Owner-occupied (homestead): $6,000 off equalized assessed value if you lived there by January 1. The township assessor starts it and no yearly application is needed.
  • Senior homestead: $5,000 more for owners who reach 65 during the tax year, applied for once at the Assessor's Office with a deed copy and proof of age.
  • Senior assessment freeze: freezes the taxable value for owners 65 or older within an income limit and needs a yearly application. The county page prints $65,000 for household income, so ask the Supervisor of Assessments which limit applies to the year you file.
  • Returning veterans: a one-time $5,000 reduction.
  • Disabled persons: $2,000 reduction, renewed each year.
  • Disabled veterans: $2,500 at 30% to under 50% service-connected disability, $5,000 at 50% to under 70%, and full exemption of the residence at 70% or more.
  • Senior tax deferral: a 3% interest loan against the home, repaid at sale or death, with a March 1 filing deadline.

sections.h2: What happens when Peoria County taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
Unpaid tax is sold at an annual sale held in early November. Registered tax buyers bid an interest figure from 0% to 9%, and the lowest bid wins. When nobody bids on a parcel, Peoria County acts as trustee for the taxing districts at 9%. The interest applies at the sale and every six months after.

The owner keeps title during the redemption period, because only the unpaid taxes are sold. The default period runs two years from the sale, though a buyer can stretch it to three. For a home of one to six units the county FAQ gives a minimum of two and a half years. If nothing is redeemed, the buyer asks a judge for a tax deed.

Redemption goes through the County Clerk at 324 Main Street, Room 101, in one payment by cashier's check, money order or cash payable to the Peoria County Clerk. Personal, business, mortgage and title company checks are refused, and there are no payment plans. The Clerk's office can be reached at (309) 672-6060 and publishes an online estimate of redemption that shows the next penalty step.

sections.h2: How do you sell a Peoria County house when tax is owed?
sections.html:
Order a payoff figure from the Treasurer for current tax and from the Clerk if any year was sold, then give both to the title company. Sold taxes are cleared by redemption at the Clerk's office, and the payoff changes every six months, so the figure should be dated close to closing.

The online property tax portal at propertytax.peoriacounty.gov shows parcel details, bills and history, and the Treasurer's page points to it for printing a copy of any bill. Check whether the parcel sits in the City of Peoria, since a township collector there takes payments separately from the county Treasurer. Mortgage escrow does not always pay on time, so confirm the last installment landed on the right parcel number.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Peoria County property tax in person?
faqs.a: At the Treasurer's office in the Peoria County Courthouse, 324 Main Street, Room G15, or through a participating bank or township collector. Bring the bill stub when paying at a bank. Banks accept payments only through the second due date, and the city of Peoria township collector handles its own residents.

faqs.q: How late can I file a Peoria County assessment complaint?
faqs.a: The window runs from June 1 until 30 days after your township's changes are published in the newspaper. For 2026 the Board of Review listed September 30 as the deadline, and it has passed. Call the Board of Review at 309-672-6022 to learn the schedule for the next cycle.

faqs.q: Can I pay only part of an installment in Peoria County?
faqs.a: No. The Treasurer returns partial payments and the tax stays unpaid until the full installment arrives, including any penalty. Penalty runs at 1.5% per month or part of a month after the due date, and electronic payments must match the exact amount or they are rejected.

faqs.q: Does an owner-occupied exemption need a yearly application in Peoria County?
faqs.a: No. The owner-occupied exemption of $6,000 is started by the township assessor and does not need an annual application. The senior homestead exemption is filed once at the Assessor's Office, while the senior assessment freeze and the disabled persons exemption must be renewed every year.

faqs.q: What is the redemption period after a Peoria County tax sale?
faqs.a: The default is two years from the sale date and a tax buyer can extend it to three. For homes of one to six units the county FAQ gives a minimum of two and a half years. Pay the County Clerk in a single payment by cashier's check, money order or cash.
